title: Booking Widget vs OTA Listing: Where Should Egyptian Operators Sell Tours?
excerpt: Viator vs direct booking for Egyptian tour operators: commission, brand control, guest data and demand compared, and where a booking widget fits.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

Quick answer

Viator versus direct booking is not either-or. An OTA such as Viator or GetYourGuide rents you ready-made demand and takes a commission on every completed booking. A booking widget on your own site sells to the visitors you already have. Most Egyptian operators need both: marketplaces for reach, a widget for the traffic your own marketing earns. One caution about our own product: the Sawa widget shows departures from Sawa's fixed catalogue, not your own tours, so it is a way to sell seats and earn from your traffic, not a storefront for your private products.

The Egyptian Travel Agents Association provides an independent place to check agency membership.

Key facts

Fact Detail
Who this is for Egyptian tour operators choosing where to sell: OTA listings (Viator, GetYourGuide), a booking widget on their own website, or both
What an OTA is An online travel agency: a marketplace that lists your tours beside thousands of others and brings its own traffic
What a booking widget is A snippet embedded on your website that shows live tours and lets visitors book without leaving your page
OTA commission Charged per completed booking. Viator's operator page gives no commission rate; industry commentary commonly puts marketplace commissions at roughly 20 to 30%
OTA cost to list Viator: pay-for-performance, with a one-time listing fee of US$29 on its operator resources page (checked November 2026). Check other marketplaces' terms directly
OTA payout timing Viator: usually every two weeks, after the experience runs (checked November 2026)
Sawa widget A snippet for WordPress, Wix, Squarespace or hand-coded sites. It shows Sawa's catalogue departures, tracked to your agency's referral code
Sawa terms No fee to join or list, and no widget fee. Sawa takes 10% of the selling price. Selling agencies earn a share of the pool for the seats they sell, paid as set in the agency agreement

Your tours are excellent, your guests leave happy, and yet most bookings arrive through an OTA after a commission comes off the top. Meanwhile your own website gets traffic that often leaves without booking. This post compares the two channels, an OTA listing and a booking widget on your own site, on the four things that matter to an Egyptian operator: commission, brand control, customer data and demand. It is a neutral comparison, not a pitch. Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), the Egypt shared-departure marketplace, has a booking widget for licensed Egyptian agencies, so we have a stake in one side, and we say so where it counts.

Viator vs direct booking: the short answer

They are different jobs, not rivals. An OTA rents you demand: it brings travellers you would never reach on your own and keeps a commission on each completed booking. A booking widget sells direct: it turns the visitors already on your website into bookings, under your own page and colours, with no marketplace standing between your visitor and the booking button. Most operators need both: marketplaces for reach, a widget for margin and repeat business.

What selling on an OTA actually costs

Listing costs little up front, and the commission starts when a booking completes. Viator describes a pay-for-performance model, "you only pay when we bring you a completed booking", with a one-time listing fee of US$29 that includes its Launch Assist onboarding. Its operator page does not publish a commission rate. Industry commentary commonly puts the big marketplaces at roughly 20 to 30%, so ask each one for the exact figure in writing. Three mechanics deserve attention before you sign.

  • You can buy visibility with commission. Viator's Accelerate programme lets operators pay a higher commission in exchange for better placement in search results. Because it works by operators outbidding each other, the benefit shrinks if most of them join.
  • You are paid after the tour. Viator pays out after the experience runs, usually every two weeks; check each marketplace's payout terms. Your van, guide and entrance tickets are paid long before the money arrives.
  • The guest books inside the platform's funnel. Payment, support and reviews run through the OTA, so ask each platform in writing what guest data you may use for your own marketing.

Reach is what you are buying. Viator's operator page describes distribution through more than 4,000 partner platforms such as Booking.com and Expedia, more than 200,000 travel agents and more than 10,000 content creators and affiliates, and says listings on Tripadvisor can send travellers to Viator.

What a booking widget on your own site does, and does not do

A booking widget embeds a live, bookable block inside your own page, so visitors reach a booking without leaving your site. Installation is the easy part. The Sawa widget is a single snippet pasted into Wix, WordPress, Squarespace or a hand-coded page. It picks up your page's colours and you can embed the whole catalogue, a single tour (the Aswan Highlights day tour is one example) or one package, each tagged with your agency's referral code.

There are two honest limits. First, a widget does not create demand. It converts the traffic your search visibility, referrals and repeat guests already bring, and if nobody visits your site it has nobody to convert. Second, the Sawa widget does not sell your own products. It shows departures from Sawa's fixed catalogue, on Sawa's calendar and at Sawa's prices, so it is a way to put those seats in front of your visitors and earn from them. If you want to sell your own private tours directly, you need a booking system of your own as well.

OTA listing vs Sawa booking widget: side by side

OTA listing (Viator, GetYourGuide) Sawa booking widget on your site
Job Brings new demand you do not have Converts demand you already have
What you sell Your own tours, in the marketplace template Departures from Sawa's fixed catalogue
Cost to start Viator: a one-time US$29 listing fee No fee to join or list; one snippet to paste
Commission Per completed booking; contract-set, commonly reported at roughly 20 to 30% Sawa takes 10% of the selling price; no widget fee
How you are paid Viator usually every two weeks Selling agencies earn a share of the pool, calculated in EGP and paid in EUR as set in the agency agreement
Brand control Your photos and text inside the marketplace template Your pages, your colours around the widget
The guest Booking, payment, support and reviews run through the platform The visitor books from your page; the booking is credited to your referral code, the contract is with the operating agency and Online Era collects the payment as its agent
Demand reach Large marketplace traffic and distribution partners Grows with your own search visibility, referrals and repeat guests
Best for New markets, first-time visitors, low season High-intent visitors and repeat guests

The balanced recommendation: treat the channels as complements. List your strongest tours on the OTAs to reach travellers who have never heard of you, and put a widget on your site to earn from the visitors your own marketing brings. The failure modes are symmetrical. An OTA-only operator rents its growth for ever, while a website-only operator caps its reach at the traffic it can earn or buy.

Four questions that decide the answer for your agency

  1. Where did last quarter's bookings come from? If marketplaces dominate, you need listings, and a widget gives your own traffic a way to convert. If your site already converts well, protect it.
  2. What does your cash flow tolerate? Marketplace payouts arrive after the tour runs, minus commission. Whichever channel you choose, plan to finance guides, transport and tickets first.
  3. How commoditised is what you sell? Inside a marketplace, a standard Giza half-day competes on price and reviews alone. On your own site, the same tour competes on your story, your service and your brand.
  4. What is a repeat guest worth to you? A traveller who books your Giza tour today may want a Nile cruise next season. Direct channels keep that relationship open; marketplace bookings usually do not.

How the Sawa widget fits an operator's site

Sawa Tours is a shared-departure marketplace. It pools travellers from several licensed Egyptian agencies onto one date of a fixed tour, and the date is confirmed, the GoAhead, when four travellers have reserved it. Groups are capped at eight, and when a departure fills a new, independent departure opens. Reserving is free, and nothing is charged before the GoAhead. Prices are fixed per traveller. Sawa Tours is operated by Online Era (registration 148500).

For an agency, the widget puts those departures on your own site. Visitors can join a group from your page, and every booking is credited to your agency's referral code. Seats sold on Sawa's departures help fill the dates on Sawa's calendar. Selling agencies earn a share of the pool for each seat sold, paid as set in the agency agreement, and Sawa takes 10% of the selling price; the operating agency, one of the licensed agencies with travellers on the date, also earns the pool share on seats it sold itself. There is no fee to join or list. The traveller's contract on a widget booking is with the operating agency, and Online Era (General Sales Agent licence 32241) collects the payment as its agent. To join, an agency needs a Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities licence, ETAA registration, passenger and liability insurance and a track record; newer agencies are welcome but must show references or a portfolio. We check the documents and confirm the licence with the Ministry. See how the widget works, how to apply and the verification form, read shared departures for Egyptian tour operators, or browse the departures already forming.

The verdict: OTA listing or booking widget?

There is no winner, only the right job for each channel. OTAs rent you reach for a commission on each completed booking. A widget puts your own traffic to work, and with Sawa it earns you a share of the pool for the seats you sell. Run both, and judge them by numbers: channel share, commission paid, repeat rate. faq.q: Should tour operators sell on OTAs or direct?
faq.a: Do both, because the channels do different jobs. OTAs such as Viator and GetYourGuide bring travellers you cannot reach alone and charge a commission on each completed booking. Selling direct through your own site keeps your brand and your pages in front of the visitor and avoids a marketplace commission. A common split is marketplaces for new markets and low season, and your own site for the visitors your marketing earns.

faq.q: What commission do Viator and GetYourGuide charge Egyptian operators?
faq.a: Viator's operator page publishes no fixed rate. Viator charges commission on completed bookings and lets operators pay more through its Accelerate programme in exchange for visibility. Industry commentary commonly puts marketplace commissions, Viator's and GetYourGuide's included, at roughly 20 to 30%. Get the exact figure in writing during onboarding.

faq.q: Who owns the customer data when a guest books through an OTA?
faq.a: The booking runs under the OTA's terms, and payment, support and reviews stay inside its system. What you may do with a guest's contact details, such as email marketing or rebooking offers, is set by each platform's supplier contract, so read it before you sign. For bookings made through the Sawa widget, the booking is credited to your referral code, the traveller's contract is with the operating agency, and Online Era collects the payment as its agent.

faq.q: Do I still need my own website if an OTA brings all my bookings?
faq.a: Yes. A website is your hedge. Marketplace rules, rankings and commission structures can change, and a listing you depend on is a listing you do not control. A site with a working booking route keeps your brand and your prices in front of the people who search for you, and it is where serious travellers check an operator before committing. The strongest set-ups feed both channels and measure each one's real margin.

faq.q: What exactly is a booking widget, and how hard is it to install?
faq.a: It is a block of embeddable code that shows live, bookable tours inside your own page. Sawa's widget is a single snippet pasted into Wix, WordPress, Squarespace or a hand-coded site, and it picks up your page's colours. You can embed the whole catalogue, a single tour or a single package, each tagged with your agency's referral code.

faq.q: Can a booking widget help me fill departures?
faq.a: On Sawa it can. Bookings made through your widget are credited to your referral code and add to the departures on Sawa's calendar. A date confirms when four travellers have reserved it, whichever agency or channel they came through, so your traffic can help a date reach the GoAhead. Seats are free to reserve until the date confirms, and groups are capped at eight.
